claim: The hybrid brain network model integrates individual structural and functional data with neural population dynamics.
source: Here, we developed a connectome-based brain network model that integrates individual structural and functional data with neural population dynamics to support multi-scale neurophysiological inference.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the developed model.

claim: Simulated populations in the hybrid model are linked by structural connectivity.
source: Simulated populations were linked by structural connectivity and, as a novelty, driven by electroencephalography (EEG) source activity.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the model architecture.

claim: Simulated populations in the hybrid model are driven by EEG source activity.
source: Simulated populations were linked by structural connectivity and, as a novelty, driven by electroencephalography (EEG) source activity.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a novel feature of the model.

claim: The hybrid model predicted subjects' individual resting-state fMRI time series over 20 minutes of activity.
source: Simulations not only predicted subjects' individual resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) time series and spatial network topologies over 20 minutes of activity
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The hybrid model predicted spatial network topologies over 20 minutes of activity.
source: Simulations not only predicted subjects' individual resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) time series and spatial network topologies over 20 minutes of activity
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: The hybrid model revealed neurophysiological mechanisms underlying resting-state fMRI oscillations.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: The hybrid model revealed neurophysiological mechanisms underlying functional connectivity networks.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations, (2) functional connectivity networks
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: The hybrid model revealed neurophysiological mechanisms underlying excitation-inhibition balance.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations, (2) functional connectivity networks, (3) excitation-inhibition balance
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: The hybrid model revealed inverse relationships between α-rhythms, spike-firing and fMRI on short time scales.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations, (2) functional connectivity networks, (3) excitation-inhibition balance, (4, 5) inverse relationships between α-rhythms, spike-firing and fMRI on short and long time scales
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: The hybrid model revealed inverse relationships between α-rhythms, spike-firing and fMRI on long time scales.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations, (2) functional connectivity networks, (3) excitation-inhibition balance, (4, 5) inverse relationships between α-rhythms, spike-firing and fMRI on short and long time scales
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: The hybrid model revealed neurophysiological mechanisms underlying fMRI power-law scaling.
source: they also revealed precise neurophysiological mechanisms that underlie and link six empirical observations from different scales and modalities: (1) resting-state fMRI oscillations, (2) functional connectivity networks, (3) excitation-inhibition balance, (4, 5) inverse relationships between α-rhythms, spike-firing and fMRI on short and long time scales, and (6) fMRI power-law scaling.
evidence: Listed as one of six empirical observations explained by the model in the abstract.

claim: Brain network models are dynamical systems of coupled neural mass models for simulating large-scale brain activity.
source: Brain network models are dynamical systems of coupled neural mass models for simulating large-scale brain activity; coupling is often mediated by estimations of the strengths of anatomical connections based on diffusion-weighted MRI data (so-called structural connectivity or 'connectomes').
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction as a definition of brain network models.

claim: Coupling in brain network models is often mediated by structural connectivity estimated from diffusion-weighted MRI data.
source: Brain network models are dynamical systems of coupled neural mass models for simulating large-scale brain activity; coupling is often mediated by estimations of the strengths of anatomical connections based on diffusion-weighted MRI data (so-called structural connectivity or 'connectomes').
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction describing typical brain network model construction.

claim: Each subject's EEG data is used to drive neural mass dynamics in the hybrid model.
source: Here, we develop a novel type of brain network model, dubbed 'hybrid model', where each subject's EEG data is used to drive neural mass dynamics (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as the defining feature of the hybrid model approach.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced ongoing subject-specific fMRI time series over a period of 20 min.
source: In brief, we were able to use the resulting hybrid models to reproduce ongoing subject-specific fMRI time series over a period of 20 min and a variety of other empirical phenomena (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a key result of the study.

claim: Previous brain network models used noise as input.
source: In contrast to previous brain network models that used noise as input, hybrid models are driven by EEG source activity (i.e. EEG sensor activity mapped onto cortical locations)
evidence: Stated in the introduction to contrast the hybrid model with previous approaches.

claim: Hybrid models simultaneously incorporate structural and functional information from individual subjects.
source: In contrast to previous brain network models that used noise as input, hybrid models are driven by EEG source activity (i.e. EEG sensor activity mapped onto cortical locations) and therefore simultaneously incorporate structural and functional information from individual subjects (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as an advantage of the hybrid model approach.

claim: Injected EEG source activity serves as approximation of excitatory synaptic input currents.
source: The injected EEG source activity serves as approximation of excitatory synaptic input currents (EPSCs), which helps to increase the biological plausibility of generated model activity (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Haider et al., 2016; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Using EEG source activity as input increases the biological plausibility of generated model activity.
source: The injected EEG source activity serves as approximation of excitatory synaptic input currents (EPSCs), which helps to increase the biological plausibility of generated model activity (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Haider et al., 2016; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Individualized hybrid models yield predictions of ongoing empirical subject-specific resting-state fMRI time series.
source: Individualized hybrid models yield predictions of ongoing empirical subject-specific resting-state fMRI time series (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a key finding.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4)
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced excitation-inhibition balance of synaptic input currents.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4), excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance of synaptic input currents
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced the inverse relationship between α-rhythm phase and spike-firing on short time scales.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4), excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance of synaptic input currents, the inverse relationship between α-rhythm phase and spike-firing on short time scales (Figure 5)
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced the inverse relationship between α-band power oscillations and spike-firing on long time scales.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4), excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance of synaptic input currents, the inverse relationship between α-rhythm phase and spike-firing on short time scales (Figure 5), and the inverse relationship between α-band power oscillations and spike-firing, respectively fMRI oscillations, on long time scales (Figure 6)
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced the inverse relationship between α-band power oscillations and fMRI oscillations on long time scales.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4), excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance of synaptic input currents, the inverse relationship between α-rhythm phase and spike-firing on short time scales (Figure 5), and the inverse relationship between α-band power oscillations and spike-firing, respectively fMRI oscillations, on long time scales (Figure 6)
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: The hybrid model reproduced fMRI power-law scaling.
source: Additionally, several empirical phenomena from different modalities and temporal scales are reproduced: spatial topologies of fMRI functional connectivity networks (Figure 4), excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance of synaptic input currents, the inverse relationship between α-rhythm phase and spike-firing on short time scales (Figure 5), and the inverse relationship between α-band power oscillations and spike-firing, respectively fMRI oscillations, on long time scales (Figure 6), and fMRI power-law scaling (Figure 7).
evidence: Listed as one of the reproduced empirical phenomena in the introduction.

claim: Simulation results show how the network interaction of neural populations leads to the emergence of empirical phenomena.
source: That is, simulation results not only predict ongoing subject-specific resting-state fMRI time series and several empirical phenomena observed with invasive electrophysiology methods, but more importantly, they also show how the network interaction of neural populations leads to the emergence of these phenomena and how they are connected across multiple temporal scales in a time scale hierarchy.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a key contribution of the study.

claim: Resting-state networks are widespread networks of coherent activity that spontaneously emerge across a variety of species in the absence of an explicit task.
source: Resting-state fMRI studies identified so-called 'resting-state networks' (RSNs), which are widespread networks of coherent activity that spontaneously emerge across a variety of species in the absence of an explicit task (Biswal et al., 1995; Fox and Raichle, 2007; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Correlations exist between fMRI and intracortical recordings.
source: Despite correlations between fMRI and intracortical recordings (He et al., 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001), EEG (Becker et al., 2011; Goldman et al., 2002; Mantini et al., 2007; Moosmann et al., 2003; Ritter et al., 2009) and magnetoencephalography (Brookes et al., 2011; de Pasquale et al., 2010) the link between RSNs and electrical neural activity is not fully understood.
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The link between resting-state networks and electrical neural activity is not fully understood.
source: Despite correlations between fMRI and intracortical recordings (He et al., 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001), EEG (Becker et al., 2011; Goldman et al., 2002; Mantini et al., 2007; Moosmann et al., 2003; Ritter et al., 2009) and magnetoencephalography (Brookes et al., 2011; de Pasquale et al., 2010) the link between RSNs and electrical neural activity is not fully understood.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: α-band activity is rhythmic activity in the 8 to 12 Hz frequency range first discovered by Hans Berger.
source: A prominent feature of electrical neural activity are oscillations in the α-band, which is rhythmic activity in the 8 to 12 Hz frequency range first discovered by Hans Berger (Berger, 1929).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with citation.

claim: Changes in information processing, attention, perceptual awareness, and cognitive performance are accompanied by rhythmic modulation of α-power and phase.
source: A growing body of research indicates that changes in information processing, attention, perceptual awareness, and cognitive performance are accompanied by rhythmic modulation of α-power and phase (Busch et al., 2009; Klimesch, 1999; Mathewson et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: An inverse relationship exists between α-band activity and neural firing.
source: The observed inverse relationship between α-band activity and neural firing is central to hypotheses on its functional significance termed 'gating by inhibition' and 'pulsed inhibition' (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Intracellular recordings showed that inhibitory events are inseparable from excitatory events, resulting in an ongoing excitation-inhibition balance.
source: Interestingly, intracellular recordings showed that inhibitory events are inseparable from excitatory events, resulting in an ongoing excitation-inhibition balance (E/I balance) (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Okun and Lampl, 2008).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Strong negative correlations exist between ongoing α-band power fluctuation and resting-state fMRI amplitude fluctuation.
source: The significance of the α-rhythm is underscored by strong negative correlations between ongoing α-band power fluctuation and resting-state fMRI amplitude fluctuation (de Munck et al., 2008; Feige et al., 2005; Goldman et al., 2002; Moosmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The key determinants of emergent power-law scaling in neural activity are unclear.
source: Lastly, despite wide-spread interest in critical dynamics (Bak, 2013), the key determinants of emergent power-law scaling, a signal pattern that is ubiquitous in nature and commonly observed in neural activity, are unclear (Beggs and Timme, 2012; Marković and Gros, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap with supporting citations.

claim: The hybrid model identified a mechanism that transformed α-power fluctuations of injected EEG source activity into fMRI oscillations.
source: Analysis led us to a mechanism that transformed α-power fluctuations of injected EEG source activity into fMRI oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a key finding from model analysis.

claim: The identified mechanism may explain the empirically observed correlation between EEG and fMRI on the longer time scale of slow fMRI oscillations.
source: The identified mechanism may explain the empirically observed correlation between EEG and fMRI on the longer time scale of slow fMRI oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Analysis led to the identification of an inhibitory effect resulting from the interaction of postsynaptic current oscillations and local population circuitry.
source: Analysis led us to the identification of an inhibitory effect resulting from the interaction of postsynaptic current oscillations and local population circuitry.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a key finding from model analysis.

claim: Prediction quality decreased when long-range coupling was deactivated.
source: Interestingly, parameter space exploration showed that prediction quality decreased when long-range coupling was deactivated (i.e. when the nodes of the long-range network were isolated from each other).
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a finding from parameter space exploration.

claim: Global coupling amplified brain oscillations in a frequency-dependent manner, amplifying slower oscillations more than faster oscillations.
source: Therefore, we interrogated the model for the influence of structural coupling on the emergence of fMRI oscillations and found that global coupling amplified brain oscillations in a frequency-dependent manner, amplifying slower oscillations more than faster oscillations, which facilitated the emergence of power-law scaling.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a finding from model interrogation.

claim: Global coupling facilitated the emergence of power-law scaling.
source: Therefore, we interrogated the model for the influence of structural coupling on the emergence of fMRI oscillations and found that global coupling amplified brain oscillations in a frequency-dependent manner, amplifying slower oscillations more than faster oscillations, which facilitated the emergence of power-law scaling.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a finding from model interrogation.

claim: The first model outcome accounts for the invasively observed inverse relationship between spike-firing and α-rhythm phase by identifying a mechanism that relates this phenomenon to ongoing E/I balance.
source: Starting with fast time scale effects, our first model outcome accounts for the invasively observed inverse relationship between spike-firing and α-rhythm phase by identifying a mechanism that relates this phenomenon to ongoing E/I balance.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a summary of the first model outcome.

claim: The second model outcome posits a neural origin of fMRI RSN oscillations by identifying an explicit mechanism that transforms ongoing α-power fluctuations into slow fMRI oscillations.
source: The second model outcome posits a neural origin of fMRI RSN oscillations by identifying an explicit mechanism that transforms ongoing α-power fluctuations into slow fMRI oscillations, which also explains the empirically observed anti-correlations between α-power and fMRI time series.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a summary of the second model outcome.

claim: The second model outcome explains the empirically observed anti-correlations between α-power and fMRI time series.
source: The second model outcome posits a neural origin of fMRI RSN oscillations by identifying an explicit mechanism that transforms ongoing α-power fluctuations into slow fMRI oscillations, which also explains the empirically observed anti-correlations between α-power and fMRI time series.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a summary of the second model outcome.

claim: The third model outcome indicates that scale invariance of fMRI power spectra results from self-reinforcing feedback excitation via long-range structural connectivity.
source: Our third model outcome indicates that scale invariance of fMRI power spectra results from self-reinforcing feedback excitation via long-range structural connectivity, which leads to frequency-dependent amplification of neural oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a summary of the third model outcome.

claim: Self-reinforcing feedback excitation via long-range structural connectivity leads to frequency-dependent amplification of neural oscillations.
source: Our third model outcome indicates that scale invariance of fMRI power spectra results from self-reinforcing feedback excitation via long-range structural connectivity, which leads to frequency-dependent amplification of neural oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a summary of the third model outcome.

claim: The hybrid model uses empirical EEG data to generate predictions of fMRI responses.
source: However, there is another perspective on this form of hybrid modeling. Because it uses empirical EEG data to generate predictions of fMRI responses, it can be regarded as a form of multimodal fusion under a generative model that is both physiologically and anatomically grounded.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as an alternative perspective on the hybrid model.

claim: The hybrid model can be regarded as a form of multimodal fusion under a generative model that is both physiologically and anatomically grounded.
source: Because it uses empirical EEG data to generate predictions of fMRI responses, it can be regarded as a form of multimodal fusion under a generative model that is both physiologically and anatomically grounded.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as an alternative perspective on the hybrid model.

claim: The hybrid model serves to fuse structural with functional data.
source: In addition, because we use connectivity constraints based on tractography, it also serves to fuse structural with functional data.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as a feature of the hybrid model.

claim: Individual hybrid brain network models were constructed for 15 human adult subjects.
source: We constructed individual hybrid brain network models for 15 human adult subjects using each subject's own structural connectomes and injected each with their own region-wise EEG source activity time courses that were acquired simultaneously with the fMRI data subsequently predicted.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: Each subject's own structural connectomes were used to construct their individual hybrid brain network model.
source: We constructed individual hybrid brain network models for 15 human adult subjects using each subject's own structural connectomes and injected each with their own region-wise EEG source activity time courses that were acquired simultaneously with the fMRI data subsequently predicted.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: Each subject's own region-wise EEG source activity time courses were injected into their individual hybrid brain network model.
source: We constructed individual hybrid brain network models for 15 human adult subjects using each subject's own structural connectomes and injected each with their own region-wise EEG source activity time courses that were acquired simultaneously with the fMRI data subsequently predicted.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: EEG source activity time courses were acquired simultaneously with the fMRI data.
source: We constructed individual hybrid brain network models for 15 human adult subjects using each subject's own structural connectomes and injected each with their own region-wise EEG source activity time courses that were acquired simultaneously with the fMRI data subsequently predicted.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: Three global parameters were tuned for each of the 15 individual hybrid brain network models using exhaustive searches.
source: Using exhaustive searches, we tuned three global parameters for each of the 15 individual hybrid brain network models to produce the highest fit between each of the subject's empirical region-average fMRI time series and corresponding simulated time series (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the parameter optimization procedure.

claim: The three global parameters were tuned to produce the highest fit between each subject's empirical region-average fMRI time series and corresponding simulated time series.
source: Using exhaustive searches, we tuned three global parameters for each of the 15 individual hybrid brain network models to produce the highest fit between each of the subject's empirical region-average fMRI time series and corresponding simulated time series (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the parameter optimization procedure.

claim: The first parameter scales the global strength of long-range coupling between regions.
source: The first parameter scales the global strength of long-range coupling between regions.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the parameters.

claim: The second parameter scales the strengths of EEG source activity inputs injected into excitatory populations.
source: The second and third parameters scale the strengths of EEG source activity inputs injected into excitatory and inhibitory populations, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the parameters.

claim: The third parameter scales the strengths of EEG source activity inputs injected into inhibitory populations.
source: The second and third parameters scale the strengths of EEG source activity inputs injected into excitatory and inhibitory populations, respectively.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the parameters.

claim: Hybrid model results were compared with the original noise-driven brain network model.
source: To better assess the quality of fMRI predictions, we compared hybrid model results with three control scenarios: (i) the original noise-driven brain network model
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the control scenarios.

claim: Hybrid model results were compared with a variant where the time steps of the injected EEG source activity time series were randomly permuted.
source: To better assess the quality of fMRI predictions, we compared hybrid model results with three control scenarios: (i) the original noise-driven brain network model, (ii) a variant of the hybrid model where the time steps of the injected EEG source activity time series were randomly permuted
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the control scenarios.

claim: Hybrid model results were compared with a statistical model where the ongoing α-band power fluctuation of injected EEG source activity was convoluted with the canonical hemodynamic response function.
source: To better assess the quality of fMRI predictions, we compared hybrid model results with three control scenarios: (i) the original noise-driven brain network model, (ii) a variant of the hybrid model where the time steps of the injected EEG source activity time series were randomly permuted and (iii) a statistical model where the ongoing α-band power fluctuation of injected EEG source activity was convoluted with the canonical hemodynamic response function (henceforth called α-regressor).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the control scenarios.

claim: Visual inspection showed good reproduction of characteristic slow (<0.1 Hz) RSN oscillations by the hybrid model and the α-regressor.
source: Visual inspection of example time series showed good reproduction of characteristic slow (<0.1 Hz) RSN oscillations by the hybrid model and the α-regressor (albeit inverted for the latter), but poor reproduction of temporal dynamics in the case of noise and random permutations models (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing visual inspection of time series.

claim: Visual inspection showed poor reproduction of temporal dynamics in the case of noise and random permutations models.
source: Visual inspection of example time series showed good reproduction of characteristic slow (<0.1 Hz) RSN oscillations by the hybrid model and the α-regressor (albeit inverted for the latter), but poor reproduction of temporal dynamics in the case of noise and random permutations models (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing visual inspection of time series.

claim: Predictions from the hybrid model correlated significantly better with empirical fMRI time series than predictions from the two random models and the α-regressor.
source: Predictions from the hybrid model correlated significantly better with empirical fMRI time series than predictions from the two random models and the α-regressor (Figure 3b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing prediction quality.

claim: Five-fold cross-validation showed no significant difference of prediction quality between training and validation data sets for the hybrid model.
source: For the hybrid model, five-fold cross-validation showed no significant difference of prediction quality between training and validation data sets (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.71, t = 0.54, Cliff's delta d = 0.0044)
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing cross-validation results.

claim: Five-fold cross-validation showed no significant difference between validation data sets and prediction quality for the full time series for the hybrid model.
source: For the hybrid model, five-fold cross-validation showed no significant difference of prediction quality between training and validation data sets (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.71, t = 0.54, Cliff's delta d = 0.0044) and between validation data sets and prediction quality for the full time series (two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.42, t = −0.2, Cliff's delta d = −0.067).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing cross-validation results.

claim: Correlation coefficients of the hybrid model were significantly larger than the control network models for most RSNs.
source: As in the case of region-wise fMRI (Figure 3b), correlation coefficients of the hybrid model were significantly larger than the control network models for most RSNs (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing RSN prediction quality.

claim: Window-wise prediction quality was highly correlated with the standard deviation of RSN temporal modes.
source: The sliding-window analyses showed that prediction quality varied over time, regions and subjects: window-wise prediction quality was highly correlated with the standard deviation of RSN temporal modes (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing sliding-window analysis.

claim: The higher the variance contributed to overall fMRI activity by an RSN in a given subject and time window, the better the prediction of empirical fMRI.
source: That is, the higher the variance contributed to overall fMRI activity by an RSN in a given subject and time window, the better the prediction of empirical fMRI, which might reflect increased synchrony of electrical activity (see Discussion).
evidence: Stated in the Results section interpreting sliding-window analysis.

claim: Epochs in the upper quartile of RSN s.d.s were significantly better predicted than epochs in the lower quartile.
source: As a consequence, epochs in the upper quartile of RSN s.d.s were significantly better predicted than epochs in the lower quartile (Figure 3d).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing quartile comparison.

claim: The maximum correlation coefficients over all tested parameters were significantly larger when empirical and simulated data sets belonged to the same subject compared to when they came from different subjects.
source: We found that the maximum correlation coefficients over all tested parameters were significantly larger when empirical and simulated data sets belonged to the same subject compared to when they came from different subjects (p<<0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Stated in the Results section assessing subject-specificity.

claim: The α-regressor showed low correlations with empirical functional connectivity.
source: Next, we compared the ability of all four setups to predict the spatial topology of empirical fMRI networks. In contrast to time series prediction, the α-regressor showed low correlations with empirical functional connectivity (FC).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing FC prediction.

claim: All three model-based approaches provided significantly better predictions of subjects' individual long-epoch FC and short-epoch FC compared to the α-regressor.
source: Compared to the α-regressor, all three model-based approaches provided significantly better predictions of subjects' individual long-epoch FC and short-epoch FC (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing FC prediction.

claim: Hybrid model simulation results correlated significantly better with empirical network topology than predictions obtained from the noise-driven model.
source: Furthermore, hybrid model simulation results correlated significantly better with empirical network topology than predictions obtained from the noise-driven model (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing FC prediction.

claim: Correlations for hybrid and random permutation models were effectively the same for FC prediction.
source: Interestingly, correlations for hybrid and random permutation models were effectively the same, likely because the long-range network dynamics, which drive the emergence of FC by structural coupling, would be relatively preserved when permuting injected activity.
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing FC prediction with interpretation.

claim: Prediction of group-average FC was better for the hybrid model compared to the α-regressor.
source: Prediction of group-average FC (all pairwise FC values averaged over all subjects) was better for the hybrid model compared to the α-regressor (Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing group-average FC prediction.

claim: The optimized hybrid model reproduced the inverse relationship between α-phase and firing rates observed in invasive recordings on the fast time scale of individual α-cycles.
source: We found that on the fast time scale of individual α-cycles (~100 ms) the optimized hybrid model reproduced the inverse relationship between α-phase and firing rates observed in invasive recordings (Haegens et al., 2011) (Figure 5a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing fast time scale dynamics.

claim: Grand average waveforms illustrate how the ongoing balancing of excitatory and inhibitory inputs generated the inverse relation between α-oscillations and neural firing.
source: Resulting waveforms illustrate how the ongoing balancing of excitatory and inhibitory inputs generated the inverse relation between α-oscillations and neural firing (Figure 5b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: EPSCs dominated the sum of synaptic input current to inhibitory populations as a result of optimizing the three model parameters.
source: As a result of optimizing the three model parameters, EPSCs dominated the sum of synaptic input current to inhibitory populations (column IV).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: Inhibitory populations' firing rates and synaptic gating closely followed the shape of EPSCs.
source: Consequently, inhibitory populations' (column V) firing rates (column VI) and synaptic gating (column VII) closely followed the shape of EPSCs.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: The waveform of inhibitory firing rates and synaptic gating closely followed injected EPSCs due to the monotonic relationship between input currents and output firing rates.
source: Because of the monotonic relationship between input currents and output firing rates (defined by Equation 3 and 4), the waveform of inhibitory firing rates and synaptic gating also closely followed injected EPSCs.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: Resulting feedback inhibition waveforms were inverted to EPSCs.
source: As increased input to inhibitory populations leads to increased inhibitory effect and vice versa, resulting feedback inhibition waveforms (IPSC, column III) were inverted to EPSCs.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: The amplitude fluctuation of EPSCs and IPSCs was proportional.
source: Furthermore, the amplitude fluctuation of EPSCs and IPSCs was proportional.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: Stronger EPSCs preceded and helped to generate stronger IPSCs.
source: That is, stronger EPSCs preceded and helped to generate stronger IPSCs.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: Excitation and inhibition were balanced during each cycle.
source: In other words, excitation and inhibition were balanced during each cycle, which is in accordance with published electrophysiology results (Haider et al., 2016; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics with supporting citations.

claim: IPSCs peaked during the trough of the α-phase and were lowest during the peak of the α-phase.
source: Consequently, IPSCs peaked during the trough of the α-phase and were lowest during the peak of the α-phase.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics.

claim: Fitting the models to fMRI activity resulted in a biologically plausible ratio of EPSCs to IPSCs, with IPSC amplitudes being about three times larger than EPSC amplitudes.
source: Fitting the models to fMRI activity resulted in a biologically plausible ratio of EPSCs to IPSCs (Xue et al., 2014), with IPSC amplitudes being about three times larger than EPSC amplitudes (compare left axes of EPSC and IPSC plots).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics with supporting citation.

claim: Excitatory populations' firing rates peaked during the trough of the α-cycle and fell to their minimum during the peak of the α-cycle.
source: Because IPSCs have dominated excitatory population inputs, excitatory populations' firing rates showed a similar shape as IPSCs, that is, they peaked during the trough of the α-cycle and fell to their minimum during the peak of the α-cycle, thereby reproducing the empirical relationship between α-cycle and firing rate (Haegens et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing model dynamics with supporting citation.

claim: Periodically alternating states of excitation and inhibition resulted from the ongoing balancing of EPSCs by feedback IPSCs.
source: In summary, the fast population activity underlying fMRI predictions showed a rhythmic modulation of firing rates on the fast time scale of individual α-cycles in accordance with empirical observations (Haegens et al., 2011). Analyses revealed that periodically alternating states of excitation and inhibition resulted from the ongoing balancing of EPSCs by feedback IPSCs, which explains α-phase-related neural firing.
evidence: Stated in the Results section summarizing the mechanism with supporting citation.

claim: Increased α-power of injected EEG source activity was accompanied by decreased firing rates, similar to intracranial recordings in monkey.
source: Similar to intracranial recordings in monkey (Haegens et al., 2011), we found that increased α-power of injected EEG source activity was accompanied by decreased firing rates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: The empirically observed inverse relationship between α-power and fMRI amplitude was observed in the form of negative correlations between the α-regressor and fMRI activity.
source: Furthermore, we also observed the empirically observed inverse relationship between α-power and fMRI amplitude (Goldman et al., 2002; Moosmann et al., 2003) in our empirical data in the form of negative correlations between the α-regressor and fMRI activity (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Input currents, firing rates, synaptic activity and fMRI activity of excitatory populations decreased in response to the α-burst.
source: After simulation, we computed grand average waveforms of model state variables over all simulated region time series and found that input currents, firing rates, synaptic activity and fMRI activity of excitatory populations decreased in response to the α-burst (Figure 6a).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing simulation results.

claim: This behavior emerged despite the fact that injected activity was centered at zero, with positive and negative deflections of input currents being balanced.
source: Notably, this behavior emerged despite the fact that injected activity (column I) was centered at zero, that is, positive and negative deflections of input currents were balanced.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing simulation results.

claim: The asymmetric response to increasing input α-power levels originated from inhibitory population dynamics: positive deflections of α-cycles generated large peaks in ongoing firing rates of inhibitory populations, while negative deflections were bounded by 0 Hz.
source: The reason for the observed asymmetric response to increasing input α-power levels originated from inhibitory population dynamics: while positive deflections of α-cycles generated large peaks in ongoing firing rates of inhibitory populations, negative deflections were bounded by 0 Hz (column V).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Average per-cycle firing rates of inhibitory populations increased with increasing α-power due to rectification of high-amplitude negative half-cycles.
source: Because of this rectification of high-amplitude negative half-cycles, average per-cycle firing rates of inhibitory populations increased with increasing α-power.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Feedback inhibition increased for increasing α-power, which led to increased inhibition of excitatory populations, decreased average firing rates, synaptic gating variables and ultimately fMRI amplitudes.
source: As a result, also feedback inhibition (IPSC, column II) had increased for increasing α-power, which in turn led to increased inhibition of excitatory populations, decreased average firing rates, synaptic gating variables (column VI) and ultimately fMRI amplitudes (column VII).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Inhibitory populations filtered negative α-deflections during epochs of increased power.
source: As in the previous example, inhibitory populations filtered negative α-deflections during epochs of increased power (column V).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Half-wave rectification led to a modulation of average per-cycle firing rates in proportion to α-power.
source: This half-wave rectification led to a modulation of average per-cycle firing rates in proportion to α-power.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The power modulation of the injected α-oscillation was introduced as a new slow frequency component into the resulting time series.
source: Consequently, the power modulation of the injected α-oscillation was introduced as a new slow frequency component into the resulting time series.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The activity of inhibitory populations can be compared to envelope detection used in radio communication for AM signal demodulation.
source: The activity of inhibitory populations can be compared to envelope detection used in radio communication for AM signal demodulation.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as an analogy.

claim: The new frequency component introduced by half-wave rectification of α-activity modulated feedback inhibition.
source: The new frequency component introduced by half-wave rectification of α-activity modulated feedback inhibition (IPSC, column II), which in turn modulated excitatory population firing rates (column V).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The large time constant of NMDAergic synaptic gating led to an attenuation of higher frequencies.
source: Furthermore, the resulting oscillation of firing rates was propagated to synaptic dynamics (column VI) where the large time constant of NMDAergic synaptic gating (τNMDANMDA100 ms vs. τGABAGABA10 ms) led to an attenuation of higher frequencies.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The low-pass filtering property of the hemodynamic response additionally attenuated higher frequencies such that in fMRI signals only the slow frequency components remained.
source: The low-pass filtering property of the hemodynamic response additionally attenuated higher frequencies such that in fMRI signals (column VII) only the slow frequency components remained, based on the assumption that neurovascular coupling was mediated exclusively by excitatory synaptic activity.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Simulated fMRI and moving average firing rate time series of the 9 Hz and the 11 Hz model had correlation coefficients r > 0.99 with the respective time series of the 10 Hz model.
source: To check whether this mechanism is robust to the choice of the frequency of the injected α-rhythm (10 Hz) we simulated otherwise identical models for artificial α-waves at 9 Hz and 11 Hz frequencies and found qualitatively identical results: simulated fMRI and moving average firing rate time series of the 9 Hz and the 11 Hz model had correlation coefficients r > 0.99 with the respective time series of the 10 Hz model.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing robustness check.

claim: Increased α-power led to increased feedback inhibition of excitatory populations introducing a slow modulation of population firing.
source: In summary, we found that increased α-power led to increased feedback inhibition of excitatory populations introducing a slow modulation of population firing, which can explain the empirically observed anticorrelation between α-power and fMRI.
evidence: Stated in the Results section summarizing the mechanism.

claim: Average power spectra of empirical fMRI data obeyed power-law distributions with exponent βemp = −0.82.
source: In accordance with systematic analyses of empirical data (He, 2011), average power spectra of our empirical fMRI data obeyed power-law distributions with exponent βemp = −0.82 (Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section with supporting citation.

claim: The power spectra of wide-band and α-band EEG have considerably smaller negative exponents than empirical fMRI.
source: Therefore, it is surprising that the power spectra of wide-band and α-band EEG have considerably smaller negative exponents than empirical fMRI (βα-band = −0.53 for α-power and βwide-band = −0.47 for wide-band power).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing power spectra comparison.

claim: Simulated fMRI had a larger negative exponent (βsim = −0.73) than the α-band power of the injected EEG source activity (βα-band = −0.53).
source: However, in agreement with empirical fMRI, our simulated fMRI had a larger negative exponent (βsim = −0.73) than the α-band power of the injected EEG source activity (βα-band = −0.53).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing power spectra comparison.

claim: Simulated fMRI had a higher negative exponent than EEG source-activity because the power of slower oscillations increased relative to the power of faster oscillations.
source: This result implies that the power-law slope increased during the process that transformed electrical band-power fluctuations into fMRI amplitude fluctuations. Indeed, comparison of power spectra indicated that simulated fMRI had a higher negative exponent than EEG source-activity, because the power of slower oscillations increased relative to the power of faster oscillations (Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Model dynamics transformed synaptic input activity such that the amplitude of output oscillations increased inversely proportional to their frequency.
source: That is, model dynamics transformed synaptic input activity such that the amplitude of output oscillations increased inversely proportional to their frequency.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: When long-range coupling was deactivated, the power-law exponent of simulated fMRI (βsim_Gzero = −0.54) was close to the exponent of the α-band power time course of the injected EEG source activity (βα-band = −0.53).
source: Interestingly, when long-range coupling was deactivated in simulations that used EEG source activity as input, the power-law exponent of simulated fMRI (βsim_Gzero = −0.54) was close to the exponent of the α-band power time course of the injected EEG source activity (βα-band = −0.53).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the effect of long-range coupling.

claim: When long-range coupling was deactivated, the amplitudes of fMRI oscillations were equally large for all oscillation frequencies.
source: When long-range coupling was deactivated, the amplitudes of fMRI oscillations were equally large for all oscillation frequencies (Figure 7b, column VII).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the effect of long-range coupling.

claim: When long-range coupling was activated, the amplitudes of slower fMRI oscillations were larger than the amplitudes of faster oscillations.
source: In contrast, when long-range coupling was activated, with everything else being identical, the amplitudes of slower fMRI oscillations were larger than the amplitudes of faster oscillations (Figure 6b, column VII), although the amplitudes of the injected artificial α-band power oscillations were equally large for all oscillations (Figures 6b and 7b, column I).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the effect of long-range coupling.

claim: Long-range coupling was responsible for increasing the power of slower oscillations relative to faster oscillation.
source: With everything else being identical, we concluded that long-range coupling was responsible for increasing the power of slower oscillations relative to faster oscillation.
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The only difference in population inputs between activated and deactivated long-range coupling was the shape of long-range input.
source: Comparison of the individual components of population inputs for activated (Figure 6b, column II) vs. deactivated (Figure 7b, column II) long-range coupling reinforced that the only difference in population inputs between both setups was the shape of long-range input.
evidence: Stated in the Results section comparing the two conditions.

claim: The amplitudes of long-range input oscillations were inversely proportional to the band-power oscillation of injected artificial α-activity.
source: The amplitudes of long-range input oscillations (Figure 6b, column II, green trace) were inversely proportional to the band-power oscillation of injected artificial α-activity.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing long-range input dynamics.

claim: Long-range input increased when α-band power decreased, while during epochs of increased α-activity long-range coupling decreased.
source: In accordance with the effect of α-band power on population activity that we described earlier, long-range input increased when α-band power decreased, while during epochs of increased α-activity long-range coupling decreased.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing long-range input dynamics.

claim: The fluctuation of long-range input was coherent with the fluctuation of IPSCs that resulted from the fluctuation of α-band power, which further amplified the effect of α-band power on population activity.
source: Consequently, this fluctuation of long-range input was coherent with the fluctuation of IPSCs that resulted from the fluctuation of α-band power, which further amplified the effect of α-band power on population activity.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: During epochs of low α-activity long-range coupling conveyed feedforward excitation that further reinforced the increasing of firing and synaptic gating.
source: During epochs of low α-activity long-range coupling conveyed feedforward excitation that further reinforced the increasing of firing and synaptic gating.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Total input currents were increased when α-band power was decreased due to consensual modulation of input currents, which resulted in larger amplitudes of firing rates, synaptic activity and fMRI.
source: Because of this consensual modulation of input currents, total input currents were increased when α-band power was decreased, which resulted in larger amplitudes of firing rates, synaptic activity and fMRI.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The large time constant of excitatory synaptic gating enabled excitatory activity to accumulate and perpetually reinforce within the long-range network.
source: Due to the large time constant of excitatory synaptic gating (τNMDA = 100 ms), long-range excitation decayed relatively slowly, which enabled excitatory activity to accumulate and perpetually reinforce within the long-range network.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The period of time for which feedforward excitation persisted was longer during slower oscillations than during faster oscillations.
source: The period of time for which this feedforward excitation persisted was longer during slower oscillations than during faster oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: Synaptic activity had more time to accumulate and was therefore larger during slower oscillations compared to faster oscillations.
source: Consequently, synaptic activity (column VI) had more time to accumulate and was therefore larger during slower oscillations compared to faster oscillations.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The amplitudes of excitatory population output reached higher values during slower oscillations than during faster oscillations when long-range coupling was activated.
source: As a result, the amplitudes of excitatory population output (columns V, VI, and VII) reached higher values during slower oscillations than during faster oscillations when long-range coupling was activated (Figure 6b).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The power of slower oscillations increases when long-range coupling is present, thereby increasing the slope of the power spectrum.
source: Accordingly, the power of slower oscillations, and therefore the slope of the power spectrum, increases in the case of long-range coupling.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing the mechanism.

claim: The effect that slower oscillations reach higher amplitudes can already be observed in firing rates and synaptic gating time series, excluding an influence of the hemodynamic forward model.
source: Note that this effect (i.e. that slower oscillations reach higher amplitudes) can already be observed in firing rates and synaptic gating time series, which excludes an influence of the hemodynamic forward model.
evidence: Stated in the Results section clarifying the mechanism.

claim: The power-law exponent of simulated fMRI depended on the balance of long-range excitation and local inhibition.
source: Screening of individual parameter spaces showed that the power-law exponent of simulated fMRI depended on the balance of long-range excitation and local inhibition: the 2D distribution of the prediction quality of fMRI time series, functional connectivity and the power-law exponent showed a characteristic diagonal pattern.
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing parameter space exploration.

claim: Increased long-range coupling required increased local feedback inhibition for producing best predictions of fMRI, FC and power-law exponents.
source: That is, increased long-range coupling required increased local feedback inhibition for producing best predictions of fMRI, FC and power-law exponents, which demonstrated the crucial role of E/I balance for the emergence of scale invariance and long-range correlations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section describing parameter space exploration.

claim: E/I balance plays a crucial role for the emergence of scale invariance and long-range correlations.
source: That is, increased long-range coupling required increased local feedback inhibition for producing best predictions of fMRI, FC and power-law exponents, which demonstrated the crucial role of E/I balance for the emergence of scale invariance and long-range correlations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Results section as a conclusion from parameter space exploration.

claim: The inferred mechanisms constitute candidate hypotheses that require empirical falsification.
source: It is important to point out that the inferred mechanisms constitute candidate hypotheses that require empirical falsification.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a caveat.

claim: The model-derived mechanisms make concrete predictions on the waveforms of different input currents, output firing rates, synaptic activities and fMRI signals, which can be empirically tested.
source: The model-derived mechanisms make concrete predictions on the waveforms of different input currents, output firing rates, synaptic activities and fMRI signals, which can be empirically tested.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a testable prediction.

claim: EEG source activity serves as an approximation of ongoing subject-specific synaptic currents.
source: Rather, EEG source activity serves as an approximation of ongoing subject-specific synaptic currents and parameter fitting is performed to tune the model to optimally explain empirical fMRI time series.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the approach.

claim: The parameter space converges for different metrics of brain activity toward a single optimal subspace indicating validity of the model.
source: We show that in fact the parameter space converges for different metrics of brain activity toward a single optimal subspace indicating validity of our model.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as evidence for model validity.

claim: Both functional datasets, EEG and fMRI, are fused within the framework of a biophysically grounded and structurally constrained model to optimally approximate the underlying behavior and parameters of the real system.
source: In our approach, both functional datasets, EEG and fMRI, are fused within the framework of a biophysically grounded and structurally constrained model in order to optimally approximate the underlying (but unobservable) behavior and parameters of the real system.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion describing the approach.

claim: Injection of source activity is a way to systematically probe sufficiently abstract neural systems while maintaining biologically realistic behavior.
source: Injection of source activity is a way to systematically probe sufficiently abstract neural systems while maintaining biologically realistic behavior.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a rationale for the approach.

claim: Imperfect reproduction of neural activity directly points to deficits in our understanding and conceptualization of large-scale brain structure and function.
source: Here, imperfect reproduction of neural activity directly points to deficits in our understanding and conceptualization of large-scale brain structure and function, which to iteratively improve is the goal of this approach.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a perspective on model limitations.

claim: The hybrid model is clearly limited by the fact that it is not an autonomous (self-contained) model of the brain, but depends on externally injected activity.
source: However, it must be noted that the hybrid model is clearly limited by the fact that it is not an autonomous (self-contained) model of the brain, but depends on externally injected activity.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a limitation.

claim: EEG-based approximation of local EPSCs is limited by the coarse spatial resolution of EEG and the inability to disentangle local EPSCs from other currents that contribute to EEG.
source: Furthermore, EEG-based approximation of local EPSCs is limited by the coarse spatial resolution of EEG and the inability to disentangle local EPSCs from other currents that contribute to EEG as all currents in the brain superimpose at any given point in space to generate a potential at that location (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a limitation with supporting citation.

claim: It is unclear how EEG exactly relates to EPSCs, that is, to which extend this approximation reflects biological reality.
source: Notably, EEG source activity can only be viewed as an approximation of EPSCs and it is unclear how EEG exactly relates to EPSCs, that is, to which extend this approximation reflects biological reality.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a limitation.

claim: Theoretical considerations suggest that excitatory postsynaptic potentials dominate current source density amplitudes.
source: Although theoretical considerations suggest that excitatory postsynaptic potentials dominate current source density (CSD) amplitudes (Mitzdorf, 1985), empirical observations repeatedly showed exceptions to this proposition.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: CSD profiles of neuronal oscillations that were entrained to rhythmic stimulus streams showed a temporal alternation of states dominated by net ensemble depolarization and hyperpolarization, indicating the contribution of IPSCs to CSD profiles.
source: For example, CSD profiles of neuronal oscillations that were entrained to rhythmic stimulus streams showed a temporal alternation of states dominated by net ensemble depolarization and hyperpolarization, indicating the contribution of IPSCs to CSD profiles (Lakatos et al., 2008; Lakatos et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: An important feature of the α-rhythm is its characteristic bistable jumping between low-power and high-power modes and a 'dwelling' in each state that follows a stretched-exponential.
source: For example, an important feature of the α-rhythm is its characteristic bistable jumping between low-power and high-power modes and a 'dwelling' in each state that follows a stretched-exponential (Freyer et al., 2009a).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The closest reproduction of EEG α-switching in the model of Freyer et al. (2011) emerged only when the uncorrelated Gaussian noise term was replaced by a state-dependent (autoregressive) noise term.
source: Importantly, the closest reproduction of EEG α-switching in the model of Freyer et al. (2011) emerged only when the uncorrelated Gaussian noise term (injected into mean membrane potentials) was replaced by a state-dependent (autoregressive) noise term, which made the injected stochastic fluctuations effectively autocorrelated.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: Cellular-level studies indicate that rhythmic GABAergic input from the interneuronal network is associated with E/I balance.
source: In line with our results, cellular-level studies indicate that rhythmic GABAergic input from the interneuronal network is associated with E/I balance (Dehghani et al., 2016) and α-related firing (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Lorincz et al., 2009; Osipova et al., 2008).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The identification of an exact physiological mechanism that explains how α-rhythms can produce an inhibitory effect remained elusive.
source: However, the identification of an exact physiological mechanism that explains how α-rhythms can produce an inhibitory effect remained elusive (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a knowledge gap with supporting citations.

claim: Mazaheri and Jensen (2010) suggest that α-related inhibition occurs due to an observed amplitude asymmetry of ongoing oscillations, also termed baseline-shift.
source: Mazaheri and Jensen (2010) suggest that α-related inhibition occurs due to an observed amplitude asymmetry of ongoing oscillations, also termed baseline-shift.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.

claim: The results suggest that a symmetrically oscillating driving signal in the α-range leads to asymmetric firing rates and synaptic currents, extending the scheme from Mazaheri and Jensen (2010) with an explicit explanation of the generation of inhibitory pulses from oscillating input currents.
source: Our results suggest, in accordance with the model from Mazaheri and Jensen (2010), that a symmetrically oscillating driving signal in the α-range leads to asymmetric firing rates and synaptic currents, but we extend this scheme with an explicit explanation of the generation of inhibitory pulses from oscillating input currents.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an extension of previous work with supporting citation.

claim: Long-range input decreased during states of high α-power and increased again when α-power decreased.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, we found that long-range input decreased during states of high α-power and increased again when α-power decreased, but further studies are required to examine the effect of α-power on long-range communication and its interaction with other frequency bands.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a finding.

claim: It is unclear to which degree non-neuronal processes affect the fMRI signal.
source: It is unclear to which degree non-neuronal processes affect the fMRI signal, as different physiological signals such as respiration and cardiac pulse rate were shown to be correlated with resting-state oscillations (Biswal et al., 1996; Power et al., 2017), which raised concerns that RSN oscillations may be unrelated to neuronal information processing, but rather constitute an epiphenomenon (Birn et al., 2006; de Munck et al., 2008; Shmueli et al., 2007; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a knowledge gap with supporting citations.

claim: Low-frequency BOLD fluctuations are strongly correlated with electrical neural activity.
source: Importantly, however, low-frequency BOLD fluctuations are also strongly correlated with electrical neural activity, which was shown by studies that analysed fMRI jointly with EEG (Goldman et al., 2002; Laufs et al., 2003; Moosmann et al., 2003), intracortical recordings (He et al., 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001) or MEG (Brookes et al., 2011; de Pasquale et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Strong temporal correlations and spatially similar correlation maps of EEG α-power, respiration and BOLD suggest that these fMRI fluctuations are not unrelated to neural activity, but may be of neural origin.
source: Similarly, strong temporal correlations and spatially similar correlation maps of EEG α-power, respiration and BOLD (Yuan et al., 2013), as well as of EEG α-power, heart rate variations and BOLD (de Munck et al., 2008) suggest that these fMRI fluctuations are not unrelated to neural activity, but may be of neural origin.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The results extend the current understanding by showing an explicit mechanism for a neural origin of fMRI RSN oscillations that explains a large part of their variance by a chain of neurophysiological interactions.
source: Our results extend the current understanding by showing an explicit mechanism for a neural origin of fMRI RSN oscillations that explains a large part of their variance by a chain of neurophysiological interactions.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a contribution of the study.

claim: The hybrid approach constitutes a multimodal data fusion approach that enables the direct characterization of the previously reported temporal correlations between BOLD and EEG signals in terms of the underlying neural activity and explicit forward models.
source: The hybrid approach therefore constitutes a multimodal data fusion approach (Friston, 2009; Valdes-Sosa et al., 2009) that enables the direct characterization of the previously reported temporal correlations between BOLD and EEG signals in terms of the underlying neural activity and explicit forward models.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The hybrid model reproduces the spatial topology of fMRI networks, which are not predicted by the α-power regressor.
source: In addition to fMRI time series, the hybrid model also reproduces the spatial topology of fMRI networks, which are not predicted by the α-power regressor.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a finding.

claim: These findings add to accumulating evidence suggesting that RSNs originate from neuronal activity rather than being a purely hemodynamic phenomenon.
source: These findings thereby add to accumulating evidence suggesting that RSNs originate from neuronal activity (Brookes et al., 2011; de Pasquale et al., 2010; Goldman et al., 2002; He et al., 2008; Logothetis et al., 2001; Mantini et al., 2007; Moosmann et al., 2003) rather than being a purely hemodynamic phenomenon that is only correlated, but not caused by it (Birn et al., 2006; de Munck et al., 2008; Shmueli et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Low-frequency fMRI oscillations may be attributed to a neural process that has a considerable state-dependent effect on neural information processing as indicated by the large modulations of neuronal firing and synaptic activity.
source: The conclusions from these results have important implications for future fMRI studies, as they implicate that low-frequency fMRI oscillations may be attributed to a neural process that has a considerable state-dependent effect on neural information processing as indicated by the large modulations of neuronal firing and synaptic activity.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an implication of the findings.

claim: Methods for physiological noise correction might remove variance from fMRI experiments that is related to neuronal activity and may therefore exclude relevant information for the interpretation of fMRI data.
source: Methods for physiological noise correction might remove variance from fMRI experiments that is related to neuronal activity and may therefore exclude relevant information for the interpretation of fMRI data.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an implication of the findings.

claim: Parameter space exploration shows that structural coupling is critical for fMRI prediction, as prediction quality decreases for sub-optimal global coupling strengths or when global coupling is deactivated altogether.
source: Parameter space exploration shows that structural coupling is critical for fMRI prediction, as prediction quality decreases for sub-optimal global coupling strengths or when global coupling is deactivated altogether (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a finding.

claim: The effect of coupling time delays was not addressed in this study, as they were non-essential for the emergence of the described phenomena.
source: In this study, we did not address the effect of coupling time delays, as they were non-essential for the emergence of the described phenomena.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a limitation.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated the important role of coupling delays for emerging large-scale dynamics.
source: Further studies are required to determine the effect of coupling delays, as previous studies demonstrated their important role for emerging large-scale dynamics (Deco et al., 2011; Jirsa, 2008, 2009).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The prediction quality of resting-state network activation time courses fluctuates over time and is highest during epochs of highest variance of the respective temporal mode.
source: We observed that the prediction quality of resting-state network activation time courses fluctuates over time and is highest during epochs of highest variance of the respective temporal mode.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an observation.

claim: During time windows when resting-state networks contribute the largest variance to whole-brain fMRI, they are the most active.
source: During these, time windows resting-state networks contribute the largest variance to whole-brain fMRI, that is, they are the most active.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: A possible explanation for higher prediction quality during high variance epochs may be that during states of asynchronous neural activity volume conduction and cancellation of electromagnetic waves decreases the ability of source imaging methods to reconstruct source activity.
source: A possible explanation may be that during states of asynchronous neural activity (i.e. when the variance of RSN temporal modes is low) volume conduction and cancellation of electromagnetic waves decreases the ability of source imaging methods to reconstruct source activity.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: The observed processes may not be specific to α-oscillations, but may apply also to other frequencies or non-oscillatory signal components.
source: It is important to note that the observed processes may not be specific to α-oscillations, but may apply also to other frequencies or non-oscillatory signal components, for example, phase-locked discharge of neurons occurs over a range of frequency bands and is not limited to the α-rhythm (Buzsaki, 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a caveat with supporting citation.

claim: The α-rhythm may be best thought of as one of several modes of brain operation, even during the so-called resting-state.
source: Furthermore, the α-rhythm, though prominent, is certainly not superior to other rhythms with respect to neuronal computation and cognition (Fries, 2015). In fact, it may be best thought of as one of several modes of brain operation, even during the so-called resting-state (Engel et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The hybrid modeling approach is not restricted to α-activity, as the injected EEG source activity was not limited to the α-band.
source: Although our analysis revolved around α-oscillations, the hybrid modeling approach is not restricted to α-activity, as the injected EEG source activity was not limited to the α-band.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a clarification.

claim: The time series correlations obtained by the α-regressor and the hybrid model are comparable, which indicates that the α-rhythm was the main driver for the hybrid model's fMRI time series prediction.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that the time series correlations obtained by the α-regressor and the hybrid model are comparable, which indicates that the α-rhythm was the main driver for the hybrid model's fMRI time series prediction.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation.

claim: Models that generate power-law distributions are often rather generic and detached from the details of the modeled systems.
source: Despite the ubiquity of scale invariant dynamics, models that generate power-law distributions are often rather generic and detached from the details of the modeled systems (Bak et al., 1987; Marković and Gros, 2014).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The precise mechanisms that lead to the emergence of fMRI power spectrum power-law scaling or the relationship between brain network interaction and fMRI power-law scaling are unclear.
source: Furthermore, the precise mechanisms that lead to the emergence of fMRI power spectrum power-law scaling or the relationship between brain network interaction and fMRI power-law scaling are unclear (He, 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a knowledge gap with supporting citation.

claim: Simulation results indicate that fMRI spectra power-law scaling is due to the observed frequency-dependent amplification of oscillatory activity in networks that contain self-reinforcing feedback excitation together with slow decay of activity.
source: Our simulation results indicate that fMRI spectra power-law scaling is due to the observed frequency-dependent amplification of oscillatory activity in networks that contain self-reinforcing feedback excitation together with slow decay of activity.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a finding.

claim: Criticality requires the existence of a control parameter that can be adjusted to move the system through a phase transition at a critical point.
source: It is important to point out that the existence of power-laws alone does not prove criticality. Rather, criticality requires the existence of a control parameter that can be adjusted to move the system through a phase transition at a critical point (Beggs and Timme, 2012).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion with supporting citation.
